tests.name: Quick Check
tests.description: Timed check on Statistical Enquiry Cycle Practice

questions.question: Q: A student wants to investigate whether Year 11 students spend more time on homework than Year 8 students. State a suitable hypothesis and identify the population.
questions.correctAnswer: Hypothesis: Year 11 students spend more time on homework per week than Year 8 students. Population: all Year 11 and Year 8 students at the school (or specified schools).

questions.question: Q: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of using a pilot study.
questions.correctAnswer: Advantage: it identifies problems with the data collection method (e.g. ambiguous questions) before the main study. Disadvantage: it takes extra time and resources, and the pilot participants cannot usually be used again.

questions.question: Q: A survey on exercise habits was conducted by posting questionnaires to 500 households. Only 120 were returned. Identify two sources of bias and explain how each affects the results.
questions.correctAnswer: 1) Non-response bias: the 380 non-responders may differ systematically (e.g. less active people may be less likely to respond), skewing results. 2) Self-selection bias: those who choose to respond may be more interested in exercise, overestimating exercise levels.

tests.name: Exam-Style Practice
tests.description: Short-answer practice on Statistical Enquiry Cycle Practice

questions.question: Q: Explain the difference between reliability and validity in the context of a statistical investigation.
questions.correctAnswer: Reliability means the investigation would produce consistent results if repeated. Validity means the investigation actually measures what it claims to measure. An investigation can be reliable without being valid (consistently measuring the wrong thing), but it cannot be valid without being reliable.

questions.question: Q: A conclusion states ‘The hypothesis is supported because the mean for Group A was higher than Group B.’ How could this conclusion be improved?
questions.correctAnswer: Include the actual values (e.g. mean A = 24.3, mean B = 18.7), mention the difference (5.6), refer to spread (e.g. overlapping IQRs mean the difference may not be significant), and acknowledge limitations such as sample size or potential bias.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response A researcher investigates the hypothesis: ‘People who walk to work have lower blood pressure than people who drive to work.’ They take a random sample of 50 walkers and 50 drivers from a city and measure their blood pressure. (a) Describe the data collection stage. (b) Write a conclusion if the median blood pressure for walkers is 120/78 and for drivers is 134/86. <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: (a) The data collection stage involves measuring the blood pressure of 100 participants (50 walkers, 50 drivers). The sampling method is random, which reduces selection bias. Data is primary (collected firsthand) and quantitative (numerical blood pressure readings). A pilot study could test the measurement protocol. (b) The data supports the hypothesis. Walkers have a lower median systolic blood pressure (120 vs 134, a difference of 14 mmHg) and a lower median diastolic blood pressure (78 vs 86, a difference of 8 mmHg). Both groups show a clear difference that suggests walking to work is associated with lower blood pressure. However, this is an observational study so causation cannot be established — people who walk may also have other healthy habits. A larger sample and controlling for confounding variables (e.g. age, diet) would strengthen the conclusion.
